A.prompt: A deposit of 200 earns 10% a year. How much interest does it earn in its second year under simple interest, and how much under compound interest?
A.answer: 20 under simple interest and 22 under compound interest, because compounding pays the rate on the whole balance of 220, the first year's interest included (slide 1, 1:38–2:12).
A.rubric: 1: 20 and 22, with the deposit against the whole balance as the reason; 0.5: one of the two amounts right.

B.prompt: You put 1000 in an account at 4% a year and leave it for two years. What does the second year pay if interest is simple, and what if it compounds?
B.answer: 40 if simple and 41.60 if it compounds, because compounding pays the rate on the whole balance, last year's interest included (slide 1, 1:38–2:12).
B.rubric: 1: 40 and 41.60, with the deposit against the whole balance as the reason; 0.5: one of the two amounts right.

C.prompt: Over its second year, how much interest does 400 at 20% a year earn when the bank pays simple interest, and how much when it compounds yearly?
C.answer: 80 with simple interest and 96 compounded, because the compound base of 480 holds the first year's 80 (slide 1, 1:38–2:12).
C.rubric: 1: 80 and 96, with the deposit against the whole balance as the reason; 0.5: one of the two amounts right.

A.prompt: A deposit of 500 earns 4% a year, compounded yearly. What does it hold after 4 years?
A.answer: About 584.93, because each of the 4 years multiplies the whole balance, past interest included, by the same 1.04 (slide 2, 5:39–6:14).
A.rubric: 1: 584.93, from 500 times 1.04 to the power 4; 0.5: right method with an arithmetic slip; 0: 580, simple interest.

B.prompt: You leave 200 in an account paying 10% a year, with the interest added to the balance each year. How much is in it after 3 years?
B.answer: 266.20, because each of the 3 years multiplies the whole balance, past interest included, by the same 1.1 (slide 2, 5:39–6:14).
B.rubric: 1: 266.20, from 200 times 1.1 to the power 3; 0.5: right method with an arithmetic slip; 0: 260, simple interest.

C.prompt: An account opens with 1000 and grows at 2% a year, compounded annually. What is the balance at the end of year 5?
C.answer: 1104.08, because each of the 5 years multiplies the whole balance, past interest included, by the same 1.02 (slide 2, 5:39–6:14).
C.rubric: 1: 1104.08, from 1000 times 1.02 to the power 5; 0.5: right method with an arithmetic slip; 0: 1100, simple interest.

A.prompt: A savings account quotes 8% a year and pays interest every quarter. What effective annual rate does it earn?
A.answer: About 8.24%, because each quarter's interest joins the balance and earns interest in the quarters after it (slide 3, 10:45–11:07).
A.rubric: 1: about 8.24%, from one plus 8% over 4, to the power 4, minus one; 0.5: right formula with an arithmetic slip; 0: 8%, the quoted rate.

B.prompt: One account pays its quoted 6% a year in two instalments. Over a full year, what rate does it really earn, as an effective annual rate?
B.answer: About 6.09%, because the second half-year pays interest on the first half-year's interest as well (slide 3, 10:45–11:07).
B.rubric: 1: about 6.09%, from one plus 6% over 2, to the power 2, minus one; 0.5: right formula with an arithmetic slip; 0: 6%, the quoted rate.

C.prompt: A loan quotes 24% a year and adds interest to the debt every month. What effective annual rate does the borrower really pay?
C.answer: About 26.82%, because each month's interest joins the debt and is charged interest in every month after it (slide 3, 10:45–11:07).
C.rubric: 1: about 26.82%, from one plus 24% over 12, to the power 12, minus one; 0.5: right formula with an arithmetic slip; 0: 24%, the quoted rate.

practice.prompt: Two accounts pay the same yearly rate on the same deposit, one simple and one compound. Why do they hold the same amount after one year but not after two?
practice.answer: In the first year there is no past interest yet, so both pay the rate on the deposit; from the second year the compound account also pays it on the first year's interest (3:06–3:54).
practice.rubric: 1: no past interest in year one, interest on interest from year two; 0.5: says compounding is faster without saying why the first year is equal.

practice.prompt: Take 300 saved at 6% a year with yearly compounding, over 3 years. Year one gives 300 × 1.06 = 318, and year two gives 318 × 1.06 = 337.08. Finish the third year: what is the final balance, and which single power of 1.06 would give it in one step?
practice.answer: About 357.30, from 337.08 × 1.06; the same balance is 300 × 1.06 to the power 3 (slide 2, 5:03–6:14).
practice.rubric: 1: 357.30 and the power 3; 0.5: one of the two; 0: 354, adding 18 each year.

practice.prompt: Someone saves 800 at 3% a year, compounded once a year, for 6 years. Set up and work out the closing balance.
practice.rubric: 1: 955.24 or 800 × 1.03 to the power 6; 0.5: right set-up with an arithmetic slip; 0: 944, simple interest.

practice.prompt: You must rank three savings accounts that pay interest on different schedules. Which single number do you work out for each one?
practice.answer: Its effective annual rate, since quoted rates on different schedules cannot be compared directly (slide 3, 12:48).
practice.rubric: 1: the effective annual rate; 0.5: 'the real rate' without naming it.
